name: Pan-Mongolism
summary: Pan-Mongolism is the call for the Mongols divided among Outer Mongolia, Inner Mongolia, Barga and Buryatia (sometimes with Tibet, Tuva and others) to be united in one Mongol state. It was pursued by the Bogd Khanate in 1911-13, by Semyonov and Neise-gegen at the 1919 Chita-Dauria conference, by Ungern in 1921 and by Inner Mongolian and Buryat nationalists in the 1920s. Its sources agree on unification and a racial or national revival but split on monarchy, the Buddhist church and the Soviet Union.
scope: The pan-Mongol unification movement 1911-1928: the Bogd Khanate's Inner Mongolia campaign, the 1919 Dauria/Chita conference and its Great Mongolia, Ungern's 1921 project, and the Inner Mongolian and Hulun Buir pan-Mongolists (Youth Party, Mersé, Fumingtai) as documented in Atwood. Excludes the Inner Mongolian autonomy movement not seeking union and the post-1920s Mongolian state's own nationalism, which rejects unification; post-1990 groups are documented too thinly to add positions. Positions outside nationhood, territory, settlement and the church-state question are not stated by its sources and are null.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: The movement's defining demand: Chita 1919 resolved on one Mongol state of Outer and Inner Mongolia, Barga and Buryatia, Ungern's 1921 letters call for 'one independent state' of all tribes of Mongol root, and the Inner Mongolian Youth Party's principle (1925) was pan-Mongolian unification.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: The Mongols were split among China, Outer Mongolia and Russia, and the Bogd government, the Chita conference and the 1921 MPRP programme all sought to bring them under one government; the movement's own documents rest the demand on that division.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Pan-Mongolists treat Mongols (Khalkha, Inner Mongols, Barga, Buryats, Daurs) as one people (ugsaga, 'race') whatever state borders divide them, which is the stated basis of the unification demand.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: The Chita conference's Great Mongolia was to merge the Mongol regions into one federal state under one government, and the 1921 MPRP programme wanted all Mongol peoples under one people's government.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The Bogd government raised an army to 'liberate' Inner Mongolia, and the Chita project claimed Inner Mongolia, Barga and Buryat lands for a Mongol state because Mongols live there.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Mongol leaders kept to supporting the 'struggle of oppressed Mongol peoples' in Inner Mongolia and Barga even when the MPRP dropped the pan-Mongol plank in 1925, and the 1911-13 Bogd government campaigned for Inner Mongolia.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: After autonomy in 1911 mass Chinese settlement on Mongol land was banned and the 1915 Kyakhta arrangements guaranteed against Chinese colonists, which the Mongol side counted as a gain; Chinese colonisation was the main grievance behind the unity cause.

majority-settlement.rationale: Mongol leaders opposed Chinese settlement of Mongol regions (banned under the autonomous government, a grievance reported on the eve of the 1919 Chita movement); the opposite of encouraging majority settlement.

national-rebirth.rationale: The Inner Mongolian pan-Mongolists' programme was 'racial revival' and awakening to avert extinction of the Mongols, and Ungern's letters call for the rebirth of the Middle Kingdom.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Split: the Bogd government and Ungern defended Mongol Buddhist and Chinggisid traditions, while Young Mongol pan-Mongolists wanted a revival freed from religious superstition and aristocratic rank.

more-religion-public.rationale: Split: the Bogd theocracy and Ungern put the Buddhist hierarchy at the centre, while Hulun Buir and Inner Mongolian pan-Mongolists were anti-clerical.

separate-church-state.rationale: Split: the 1911 Bogd Khanate was a theocracy, whereas the Inner Mongolian pan-Mongolist youth and the later MPRP were anti-clerical.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Split: the Bogd government and Ungern kept the lama hierarchy at the top, while the Hulun Buir pan-Mongolists and MPRP-aligned strands opposed clerical power.

clerical-rule.rationale: Split: the Bogd Khanate was headed by an incarnate lama, but other pan-Mongolist strands rejected clerical rule.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Split: the Bogd Khan and Ungern (who wanted the Qing dynasty restored over Central Asia) were monarchists, while Young Mongol pan-Mongolists wanted the hereditary nobility abolished.

elective-rulers.rationale: Split: the Bogd Khanate and Ungern stood for inherited and incarnate rulers, the Inner Mongolian pan-Mongolist left for ending hereditary estates.

defeat-communism.rationale: Split: Ungern called communism a godless Western plague to be crushed, while Fumingtai and Oljeijirgal were friendly to the Soviet Union and the MPRP pan-Mongolists worked with the Comintern.

revolution-justified.rationale: Split: Ungern and the Bogd camp condemned revolution, while the Inner Mongolian pan-Mongolist left and the MPRP made a revolution.
